chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
title: The Seattle amplifier story and the guitar players' hour off
summary: In Seattle, probably 1938, guitar players were given an hour off to hear him with his amplifier, and his amp failed on stage.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: I think that was in the '30s, because at the time, when I was playing, there wasn't anybody playing. I remember that now, because I came from Seattle, Washington, came from Vancouver, B.C. with a girls' band. And I was going to play Seattle, Washington, coming out of Vancouver, B.C. And the way they had it, my band was going at 12:00 at night so the musicians (inaudible). And I'll never forget it. In Seattle, Washington, they let all the guitar players off one hour, from 12:00 to 1:00, and they announced it that all the guitar players can be off in all the clubs. And the boss allowed people to come hear me because I had out that Honey, Keep Your Mind on Me, with that electric thing? But that was accoustic. But I had got (inaudible) electric. I had an amplifier then. I remember, I set up on the stage and they used to blow the lights out. Man, they'd want me to set up the amplifier with two tubes in it. I said, if we cover this box, the guys won't bother me, they'd never want that amplifier. I'll never forget it. All the guitar players in town was back there in the club, come in free, big club. Say, the only thing I want out of it was listening. And -- because (unintelligible) that year, '38. But Christian went with Goodman that year.
See? And that's the reason I remember, somewhere in there, and then I walked out there -- I had the

band to play and make a big introduction. After the introduction, I was supposed to come in with something on that guitar, you know. I come down and nothing coming out of the (unintelligible). And they start to call up, because they had amplifiers then. And the guy called up (unintelligible). You ought to seen the guys jumping up and getting into the cars, "we'll go get him an amplifier."

So that's the only reason I (unintelligible). I played two numbers and that was it. But the guys had never -- they hadn't heard anybody play the way I played, but they had the instruments, they couldn't do nothing with them. It was just minor then.
